description: I’m a CSE student passionate about AI/ML, software engineering, data science, and solving real-world problems. For NASA Space Apps 2026, I’m working on the Fire Flame challenge, exploring how satellite data, ML, and visualization can help understand and respond to fires. I’m looking for teammates skilled in AI/ML, GIS, remote sensing, UI/UX, data visualization, research, or presentation.
summary:
Flamme is a web dashboard that turns NASA’s scattered microgravity combustion data into fire-safety insight for people planning spacecraft and lunar or Mars habitats. It is our entry to the Flame in Freefall challenge.

We built a catalog of 115 findings from 24 NASA PSI investigations and NTRS reports, each linked to its source. The app ranks them for a chosen crew environment (ISS, Moon, Mars), maps where the evidence has gaps, and shows what varied between tests inside each investigation. Rankings can also be filtered by detection, suppression, ventilation or life-support equipment.

An SI layer lets users ask plain-language questions, such as whether a fire would self-extinguish at 30% oxygen. A language model reads the question, then writes a short answer using only the top-ranked findings. It cites each one, and if the service is unavailable the app falls back to keyword matching. Two small models trained on real NASA test data, one for liquid droplets (FLEX) and one for gaseous fuels (CFI-G, up to 85% oxygen), sit beside a 3D lab. They refuse to predict outside the conditions NASA tested, and we report that CFI-G is no better than always guessing “ignites” on accuracy.

This matters because exploration atmospheres change how fires behave, and the evidence is hard to compare across experiments.
details:
What it does and how it works

Flamme turns NASA’s microgravity combustion data into something a safety engineer can search, compare and question. We assembled a catalog of 115 findings from 24 NASA PSI investigations and NTRS technical reports. Each finding keeps its source file, page and caveat.

  • Rankings: the user picks a crew environment (ISS, transit, Moon, Mars) or sets oxygen, pressure and gravity. Each finding is scored on how well it matches those conditions, how severe it is and how strong the evidence is. The same formula runs in a Python script and in the browser.
  • Filters and export: Rankings can be filtered by theme or by equipment type (detection, suppression, ventilation, life support) and exported as CSV or JSON.
  • Investigations: the page lets users compare up to four investigations. Each one with a PSI test table shows which conditions varied between its tests and which stayed the same, computed from the cleaned PSI data.
  • Gap map: it shows which gravity and oxygen combinations NASA has tested and which it hasn’t.
  • Ask: users type a plain-language question. A language model reads it into conditions, and Flamme ranks the findings. The model then writes a short answer from only the top five findings and cites them. The browser drops any citation the model invents. If the service is down or rate-limited, the page falls back to a keyword parser and says so.
  • Lab: a 3D chamber with two trained models next to an illustrative one. One model is for liquid droplets (FLEX, 274 tests). The other is for gaseous flames (CFI-G, 325 tests, oxygen up to 85%). Both refuse to predict outside the conditions NASA tested and link to the closest real test.

Benefits and intended impact

NASA’s evidence is spread across drop towers, the ISS and Saffire flights, and each source records conditions differently. Flamme lets a designer see which evidence applies to a given cabin atmosphere and where nothing has been tested. That matters for Moon and Mars atmospheres, because no partial-gravity fire tests exist. We want it to support evidence review for exploration fire safety, not replace testing or certification.

Tools

  • Front end: React 19, Vite, React Router and Three.js, deployed on Vercel.
  • Backend and LLM: a Vercel serverless function calling the Groq API (openai/gpt-oss-120b).
  • Data and models: Python with pandas, NumPy and scikit-learn for data cleaning and training. The CFI-G model uses NumPy only. The models ship as plain coefficients, so the browser only does the arithmetic.
  • Claude (Anthropic): it helped write code, scripts and text. This is disclosed in the README and in the app.

What’s creative

  • Grounded answers: the AI summarizes only the evidence the ranking hands it, and every claim is checked against that evidence.
  • Honest models: the app says where the models fall short. CFI-G ranks flames better than chance but doesn’t beat always guessing “ignites” on accuracy.
  • Visible limits: the evidence gaps and the “outside the tested range” states are shown, not hidden.

What we considered

  • Provenance: every number can be traced to a NASA file and row.
  • Mismatched data: inverse-flame oxygen is the burner stream, not the cabin atmosphere, so each flame type is only predicted within its own range.
  • Cleaning: a few table cells look like entry errors, such as oxygen values of 2100% and 3400%. We left them out and said so on the page.
  • Public endpoint: the AI endpoint has a rate limit and a cache.
  • Safety wording: the app states it is not a NASA product, is not NASA-endorsed, and must not be used for certification or operational safety decisions.
